body: Pleasant Park is the biggest pickleball site in Apex and the one you should think hardest about before setting off. The town's court table gives it six courts, more than anywhere else in town, and its own page confirms "6 Pickleball courts" in the features list. It is also the only Apex venue the town marks as unlit, and the only one that publishes separate court hours: "Basketball and Pickleball Court Hours: Sunrise to 30 minutes after Sunset", against park hours of 5:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. So the largest concentration of courts in Apex is shut when the three smaller lit sites are still open. The park is Apex's newest, a 92-acre facility built around a 1.5-acre Enchanted Forest playground with nine inclusive play villages, and it carries six lighted rentable multi-purpose fields, four tennis courts, four basketball courts, two shelters and a field house with rentable meeting rooms. One genuinely unusual thing: the town publishes a live court occupancy feed for the pickleball courts, which no other operator in this directory does.

3400 Pleasant Plains Rd., Apex, NC 27502. The town publishes no parking capacity or restriction for the park, though its own FAQ list includes the question "Can I park along Pleasant Plains Road?", which suggests the question comes up; we have not read the answer and will not guess at it. Restroom facilities are on site and open from 6:30 a.m. with the courts and fields, an hour after the park itself opens at 5:30 a.m. Note that Splashlantis, the park's splash pad, was closed for maintenance when we checked on 3 September 2026, with no reopening date published — that does not affect the courts but it will affect what else is going on around them.

Six courts and no floodlights. Check the live occupancy feed before you drive out, then check the sunset: court hours here end thirty minutes after it, which in December is mid-afternoon. Nothing at this park can be booked — the town states courts cannot be reserved by players or groups, only by its own department for sponsored programmes, and that organised league play and private lessons outside town programming are not allowed per Town Ordinance. So a busy Saturday is first-come, first-served all the way down. What the town does not publish for this venue is a surface material, whether nets are provided, or any fee, so all three read "Not verified yet" here rather than being filled in with something plausible.

Kelly Road Park is a 25-acre neighbourhood park in Apex whose four pickleball courts are shared with junior tennis. The town's table lists it with four courts and marks it lit; the park's own features list puts it more precisely as "4 junior tennis / pickleball courts", which tells you what you are actually playing on — junior-sized tennis courts carrying pickleball lines, rather than courts built for the game. Alongside them the park has one full-size tennis court, one basketball court, a lighted softball field, two playgrounds split by age, a picnic shelter with a grill, restroom facilities and a trailhead onto the Beaver Creek Greenway. It is one of three Apex venues that run 6:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. year round, which together with the lights makes it a genuine evening option in a town whose biggest site closes at dusk.

1609 Kelly Road. The town publishes no parking guidance for this park — no lot, no capacity, no restriction — so we cannot tell you where to leave a car, only that the page does not say. Restroom facilities are listed among the park's features. Be aware that the KidsTowne playground here was in the design phase of a renovation as of 20 August 2026, so there may be work on site; the town has published no completion date.

Four lit courts, shared with junior tennis, open 6:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. year round. Expect the sharing to matter: a junior tennis session has as much claim on the surface as you do, and with four courts a queue builds quickly at a neighbourhood park. Nothing here can be reserved — the town's policy is that courts cannot be booked by players or groups at all, only by its own department for sponsored programmes, and organised league play and private lessons outside town programming are not permitted under Town Ordinance. The town does not publish a surface material for these courts, whether nets are provided, or any fee. One small note on the records rather than the place: the commercial dataset this directory started from holds two separate rows for this park, "Kelly Road Park" and "Apex Kelly Rd Park", both claiming four courts. They are the same park. We publish one venue.

The Seymour Athletic Fields are the active half of Apex Nature Park, a site of over 160 acres that the town splits into two distinct sections with separate entrances. Section one, at 2500 Evans Road, is where the sport is: lighted tennis courts, lighted pickleball courts, lighted multipurpose fields, sand volleyball, a multi-age playground and a restroom. Section two, at 2600 Evans Road, is the quieter half — an outdoor amphitheatre, a disc golf course, a dog park, environmental education stations and paved paths. The town's court table gives the pickleball count as four and marks it lit, and notes the courts are also used for junior tennis; the park's own page confirms "Lighted pickleball courts" among the Seymour features but does not put a number on them, which is why the count here rests on the table. The full name the town uses is Seymour Athletic Fields at Apex Nature Park.

2500 Evans Road — and the entrance matters more here than at most parks. The town states there are parking lots at both entrances and a paved walkway connecting the two sides, so arriving at 2600 Evans Road for the pickleball means a walk across the park. A restroom facility is listed in the Seymour section, and a second one on the nature park side. Park hours run 5:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. year round, with the fields, courts and restrooms opening at 6:30 a.m.

Four lit courts shared with junior tennis, open 6:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. As everywhere in Apex, they cannot be booked: the town states courts are not reservable by players or groups, only by its department for sponsored programmes, and organised league play and private lessons outside town programming are not allowed per Town Ordinance. With lights and a 10 p.m. close this is one of the three Apex sites that work after dark, against Pleasant Park's six unlit courts. The town publishes no surface material for these courts, no statement about nets and no fee. If you want the quieter side of the park afterwards — the disc golf, the amphitheatre, the dog park — it is a paved walk away rather than a drive.

Apex Community Park is the town's big general-purpose park — 160 acres with a lake of over 50 acres — and its pickleball is the smallest of the four outdoor sites at three courts. What it gives up in number it gains in certainty and in light: the park's own features list states "3 lighted pickleball courts" in a single line, which is the most direct statement of both count and lighting anywhere in Apex, and the town's court table agrees. Around them the park carries six tennis courts, two basketball courts, three sand volleyball courts, two street hockey rinks, three ball fields with batting cages reserved for league play, a fitness course, a playground with swings, restroom facilities and more than three miles of trails. There is a wheelchair-accessible fishing dock — the park is part of the NC Wildlife Community Fishing Program and is stocked with channel catfish — and a launch for canoes, kayaks and paddleboards up to fourteen feet.

2200 Laura Duncan Road for the park entrance. There is a second published entrance, the Lake Trail entrance at 1808 Lake Pine Drive, which is the one to avoid if you are heading for the courts. No parking capacity or restriction is published for either. Restroom facilities are on site, and park hours are 6:30 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. year round. A renovation of the playground next to the baseball fields was in its design phase as of 20 August 2026, adding ADA-accessible ramps and walkways to the adjacent parking lots, with no completion date announced.

Three lit courts, open until 10 p.m. year round, in a park with a great deal else going on. Three courts is few enough that a busy evening will mean waiting, and there is no way to shorten the wait by booking: the town states courts cannot be reserved by players or groups, only by its own department for sponsored programmes, and bans organised league play and private lessons outside town programming under Town Ordinance. What the town does not publish here is a surface, a statement about nets, or a fee — which is a striking gap given how precisely it describes everything else in this park, down to the maximum length of a boat you may launch on the lake.

The John M. Brown Community Center holds the only indoor pickleball courts verified anywhere in this directory. Four of them, on the Town Hall campus at 53 Hunter Street, and the town's court table marks them Indoor and lit. It also attaches the restriction that defines the venue: they are "available only for ages 55+, during designated open gym hours". This is not a drop-in gym for everyone, and the town publishes a separate Senior 55+ Indoor Pickleball Calendar for what hours those are. The facility was formerly known as the Apex Community Center, which is the name the commercial dataset this directory started from still uses for it — the town's own statement of the rename is what let us tie the two records to one place, and the counts agree at four. The building itself is a rentable community centre with three large rooms separated by partition walls, an arts and crafts room and a catering kitchen, with rates from $24 to $101 an hour depending on the room, the day and whether you live in Apex.

53 Hunter Street, on the Town Hall Campus. The town publishes no parking guidance specific to the centre and no restroom flag we could verify, though it is a staffed public building with rentable rooms. The building's own opening hours are Monday to Friday 8 a.m. to 9 p.m., Saturday 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Sunday 1 p.m. to 6 p.m., closed on Sundays from June through Labor Day. Reservations for rooms are handled in person between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. on weekdays.

Indoor pickleball, if you are 55 or over and you come at the right time. We have deliberately not published opening hours for this venue, and the reason is worth stating: the building's hours are known, but pickleball runs "during designated open gym hours", which is a subset of them. Publishing the building's hours as the court's hours would tell a reader they can play at times when they cannot. Check the Senior 55+ Indoor Pickleball Calendar the town publishes for this facility before travelling. As everywhere in Apex, the courts cannot be reserved by players or groups. The town publishes no surface material, no statement about nets and no fee for the pickleball itself, though it publishes room rental rates for the rest of the building in detail.

The Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway is the largest verified pickleball site in Cary and the only one the town describes as lit. Its features list is unusually precise about the difference between its two racquet sports: "Lighted Tennis Court: Reservable 16 hours in advance" sits directly above "Lighted Pickleball Courts: Non-reservable, first-come, first-served". So the sport you can book here is tennis, and the one you cannot book is pickleball — which, counter-intuitively, is the better deal for a player turning up unannounced, because nobody can have reserved the courts out from under you. The count comes from a different page: the park's own entry confirms the courts exist and are lit but gives no number, while the Cary Tennis Park facility page lists this site among its satellite locations as "McCrimmon Park (3870 Cary Glen Blvd.) Six Lighted Tennis Courts and Six Lighted Pickleball Courts". Six is what we publish. The park is a 20-acre site at the south-east corner of Green Level Church Road and McCrimmon Parkway in north-west Cary, opened out of a 2019 parks bond, and the town gave it a nature theme because of the creeks and steep slopes across the site.

3870 Cary Glen Blvd, in north-west Cary. The town publishes no parking guidance for this park — no lot location, no capacity, no time limit — which is a gap worth knowing at the busiest pickleball site in town. Restrooms are listed among the park's features. Paved loop trails run through the site, and there is a community garden that is closed to the public except during events. Note the naming: the town calls this park "Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway" on its own page and "McCrimmon Park" on the Cary Tennis Park page. They are the same place.

Six lighted courts, first-come and first-served, with no way to reserve them. This is where Cary runs its Monday evening open play, 7 to 9 p.m., and the town's leagues use these courts periodically for match play alongside Cary Tennis Park — so an evening visit may find a league on. Park hours are sunrise to sunset, extended in lighted areas where visitors are taking part in an approved extended-use activity until thirty minutes after it ends or 11 p.m., whichever comes first. Read that carefully: the extension is tied to an approved activity, not to casual play, so lights do not automatically mean a late game. What the town does not publish for this venue is a surface material, whether nets are provided, or any fee — so all three read "Not verified yet" here rather than being filled in with something plausible.

Ed Yerha Park is the park the Town of Cary points to first: its page opens by saying the park "features Cary's outdoor Pickleball courts, where everyone is welcome and encouraged to play". There are three of them, stated plainly in the features list as "Three pickleball courts", alongside one basketball slab and one open play field. The park was formerly White Oak Park and was renamed for Ed Yerha, a councilmember from 2012 to 2022 who volunteered for the town for more than two decades, helped form Cary's first Senior Advisory Board and made a series of local history videos for the town's 150th anniversary. The old name has not entirely gone: the town's open data still carries the White Oak Park URL on the same map point, which is how we matched the two records to one place. For a player, this is a small, straightforward, purpose-signposted pickleball venue rather than a large one — three courts, restrooms, a picnic shelter, and a town that describes it as the home of its outdoor pickleball.

1216 Jenks Carpenter Road. The town publishes no parking information for this park at all — not a lot, not a capacity, not a restriction — so we cannot tell you where to leave a car, only that the page does not say. Restrooms are on site and the town's status board lists them as open. There is a picnic shelter, available by reservation, and a playground.

Three courts on a first-come, first-served basis: the town's own status board for the park reads "Pickleball Courts Open - First Come, First Served", and there is no reservation system for them. Come in daylight. The park's hours are published as "Sunrise to Sunset" flatly, with none of the extended-activity clause that Carpenter Park and the McCrimmon Parkway park carry, and nothing on the page states that these courts are lit — so we record lighting as not verified and you should plan for the sun. The basketball slab is listed separately from the pickleball courts, which suggests the two are not sharing a surface here the way they do at Carpenter Park, though the town does not say so outright and we are not going to claim it did. No surface, no nets and no fee are published for this venue.

Carpenter Park is a 16-acre neighbourhood park in north-west Cary whose three pickleball courts share their surface with basketball. The town states it directly in the features list — "Multi-Sport Courts: Basketball & 3 Pickleball Courts" — which is a useful piece of honesty: you are playing on multi-sport slabs, and the lines under your feet are not all yours. The park is also a memorial site, for Flights AE3379 and AE3378, and it holds a central pond with an earthen dam, a community garden, a terraced lawn, preserved forest and pedestrian trails. It is the one venue in this entire directory whose operator tells you how many cars fit, which is why it earns a mention on the city page's parking note that nowhere else in Cary does.

4420 Louis Stephens Drive, and the town publishes "Parking for 30 Cars". That is the only parking capacity any operator in this directory has given us, and it is worth reading against what else is at the park: a playground, a community garden, a picnic shelter, trails and a memorial all draw on the same thirty spaces as the courts. There is a restroom structure on site. No time limit, permit requirement or fee is published for the parking.

Three courts, shared with basketball, on multi-sport slabs. Expect that sharing to matter — a basketball game has as much claim on the surface as you do, and with three courts a queue builds quickly at a neighbourhood park this size. Park hours are sunrise to sunset, extended in lighted areas where visitors are taking part in an approved extended-use activity until thirty minutes after it ends or 11 p.m. at the latest. That clause refers to lighted areas of the park in general; nothing on the page states that these particular courts are lit, so lighting here is recorded as not verified rather than as present. The picnic shelter at the playground is first-come, first-served rather than reservable. No surface material, nets or fee is published for the courts.

Clarks Creek Park has eight pickleball courts, the most of any park verified in Charlotte, on Hucks Road in the north of the city. Mecklenburg County does not say "eight" anywhere. It says "Clarks Creek Park: Courts 1-5" under Reservable Courts and "Clarks Creek Park: Courts 6-8" under Open Play Courts, which between them name courts one to eight with nothing missing and nothing counted twice — so eight is what the county is telling you it has, one court at a time.

That split is the useful part. Five of the eight can be booked for what the county calls a small fee; three are permanently open play and cannot be reserved by anyone. Three guaranteed walk-up courts is more than any other Charlotte park keeps back, which makes this the best bet in the city for turning up without a plan.

One caution about the name. The City of Charlotte parks layer holds three separate records with Clarks Creek in the title: this park at 5435 Hucks Road, Clarks Creek Nature Preserve directly across the road at 5434 Hucks Road, and Clarks Creek Greenway Park several miles away on Mallard Creek Road. Only this one has pickleball.

5435 Hucks Rd, Charlotte, NC 28269, in the north of the city. The county publishes no parking information for this park — no lot, no capacity, no restriction. It does warn that its neighbourhood parks "do not typically have parking or restroom features", but Clarks Creek is classified as a Community park rather than a neighbourhood one, so that warning most likely does not apply here. Most likely is not a source, so we have recorded nothing either way about parking or restrooms. Watch the address when navigating: Clarks Creek Nature Preserve is at 5434 Hucks Road, one digit and one side of the road away.

Eight courts, five bookable and three always open. The county says its local park courts "are always open for play" and that any court not on its reservable list is "non-reservable and open to the public on a first come, first serve basis", so courts 6, 7 and 8 here cannot be taken from you by a booking. What it does not publish is anything about the courts themselves: no lighting information, so we cannot tell you whether this park is usable after dark; no surface material; no statement about nets; and no price for the reservations it charges for. All of those read "Not verified yet" on this page. Charlotte is the only city in this directory where the operator publishes no lighting data at all, and at an eight-court site that is the gap you will feel most.

Freedom Park is one of Mecklenburg County's Regional parks and one of Charlotte's best-known green spaces, and its pickleball courts are numbered 11 to 16. That is not an error and it is the most interesting thing on this page. Courts 1 to 10 at Freedom Park are tennis courts, listed separately higher up the same county page, and the county runs a single numbering series across both sports at this site rather than restarting it for each. You can read the order the facilities arrived in straight out of the numbers.

Six pickleball courts, then: 11, 12, 14 and 15 are reservable for a small fee, and 13 and 16 are permanently open play. Note how they interleave — the county has not simply reserved a contiguous block and left the ends, it has taken four and left two spaced through the run. The two lists still reconstruct a complete 11 to 16 with nothing missing and nothing counted twice, which is the check that the reading is right.

As a Regional park rather than a neighbourhood one, Freedom Park sits outside the county's blanket warning that its smaller parks lack parking and restrooms.

2435 Cumberland Ave, Charlotte, NC 28203, south of uptown. The county publishes no parking guidance for the park and no capacity or restriction, which for a Regional park drawing visitors from across the city is a meaningful gap. Nothing on the county's courts page states whether there are restrooms at the courts themselves.

Six courts, four bookable and two always open, sharing a site with ten tennis courts. Expect the park to be busy in a way the court count alone does not convey — this is a destination park rather than a neighbourhood one. The county states that any court not on its reservable list is open on a first-come, first-served basis, so courts 13 and 16 are yours if they are free. What the county does not publish for this venue is lighting, surface, nets, opening hours or the price of a reservation, so all of those read "Not verified yet" here. If you are looking for the courts on arrival, the numbering is your friend: the pickleball is the 11-to-16 block.

Clanton Park is a Community park in south-west Charlotte with six pickleball courts, numbered 1 to 6. Four of them — courts 1 to 4 — are reservable for what Mecklenburg County calls a small fee, and courts 5 and 6 are permanently open play, so there are always two courts here that nobody can book ahead of you.

The park sits on Clanton Road near the Revolution Park area. The City of Charlotte parks layer holds a separate record for Clanton Park Community Garden at a different address on Revolution Park Drive, so if you are searching by name you may find two things; the courts are at 1520 Clanton Road.

That address is worth a note of its own. The commercial dataset this directory started from carries a Clanton Park row with the postcode 28208. The county's own parks layer gives 28217 for 1520 Clanton Road. We publish 28217, because it comes from the operator's record rather than from an aggregator, and because a fact with a source beats a field without one.

1520 Clanton Rd, Charlotte, NC 28217. No parking information is published for this park — no lot, no capacity, no restriction. The county's warning that neighbourhood parks lack parking and restrooms does not formally apply here, since Clanton is classified as a Community park, but the county publishes nothing positive about either facility at this site so we have recorded nothing.

Six courts, four bookable and two open play. As at every Mecklenburg park in this set, the county keeps some back: courts 5 and 6 cannot be reserved by anyone, which the county describes as first come, first serve. Nothing is published about lighting, surface, nets, hours or the reservation fee, so all of those read "Not verified yet". The county does say generally that its local park courts "are always open for play", which is a statement about access rather than a timetable — it does not tell you when the park closes, and no source we have read does.

Martin Luther King Jr. Park is a Community park in west Charlotte with six pickleball courts, numbered 1 to 6. Mecklenburg County writes it "MLK Park" in its court lists and "Martin Luther King Jr. Park" in the city parks layer; we publish the full name.

The reservable split here is the most scattered of the five Charlotte parks. Courts 2, 3, 5 and 6 can be booked; courts 1 and 4 are permanently open play. So the two walk-up courts are not a block at one end but are spaced through the run, which suggests the county is deliberately distributing guaranteed access across the facility rather than corralling it. The two lists still rebuild a complete 1 to 6.

If you are searching by name, note that the city's parks layer also holds a separate record for Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School on Bilmark Avenue. The park with the pickleball courts is on Ravencroft Drive.

2600 Ravencroft Dr, Charlotte, NC 28208. The county publishes no parking guidance, capacity or restriction for this park, and nothing about restrooms at the courts. As a Community park it falls outside the county's general warning about neighbourhood parks lacking both, but that is an inference from a size class rather than a statement about this site, so we have recorded neither.

Six courts, four bookable and two — courts 1 and 4 — always open play. The county states that any court not on its reservable list is open first come, first served, so those two cannot be taken by a booking. Everything else about the courts is unpublished: no lighting, so we cannot say whether evening play is possible; no surface material; no statement about nets; no opening hours; and no price for the reservations. All read "Not verified yet" here. That is five blanks on one venue, and it is a fair picture of what Mecklenburg County publishes about its courts as against what Raleigh and Apex publish about theirs.

Colonel Francis J. Beatty Park is the smallest pickleball site verified in Charlotte at three courts, and the only one where a walk-up player is competing for a single court. Mecklenburg County lists courts 2 and 3 as reservable and court 1 as open play — so of the three, exactly one can never be booked.

The numbering repeats the pattern seen at Freedom Park. Beatty also appears on the county's tennis lists, with courts 5 and 6 reservable and court 4 as open play, so the site runs one series across both sports: pickleball is 1 to 3 and tennis is 4 to 6. It is a Regional park, the county's largest size class, in the far south-east of the city.

This is also the venue where the records disagree about where it is. Its postcode is 28105, which is a Matthews mailing ZIP, while the City of Charlotte parks layer labels its city as Charlotte. We put the park's published coordinates through the US Census geocoder, which places the point inside the incorporated place of Charlotte, in Mecklenburg County. A mailing address and a municipal boundary are different things, and at this park they disagree.

4330 Weddington Rd, Charlotte, NC 28105, in the far south-east of the city near Matthews. If you are searching for it, expect listings to place it in Matthews on the strength of the postcode; the park itself is inside the Charlotte city limits. The county publishes no parking guidance, capacity or restriction for the park, and nothing about restrooms at the courts.

Three courts, two bookable and one always open. That ratio matters more here than anywhere else in Charlotte: if both reservable courts are booked, a walk-up player is waiting for court 1 alone. The county publishes no lighting, surface, nets, hours or reservation price, so all of those read "Not verified yet". The site also carries three tennis courts numbered 4 to 6, sharing the same numbering series, so if you are looking at signage on arrival the pickleball is the 1-to-3 end. As a Regional park it sits outside the county's warning that smaller neighbourhood parks typically lack parking and restrooms, though the county states nothing positive about either here.

Columbia Park holds eight pickleball courts, equal-largest in Portland for year-round play and one of only four sites the parks department names as sanctioned pickleball parks. That designation is worth more here than it sounds. Portland has written down a rule that it stripes pickleball only where courts sit roughly 300 to 600 feet from housing, and it names Columbia, Pier, Sellwood and Gabriel as the parks where that condition is met. Columbia is therefore not a tennis court someone has borrowed — it is one of the handful of places in the city where the department has decided pickleball belongs. The courts are hard-surfaced, described by the city with permanent lines, and free.

4503 N Lombard St, Portland, OR 97203, in North Portland — the address itself says so, and the Census geocoder places it in Multnomah County. Lombard is a major east-west arterial across the north of the city, which makes the park easy to find and says nothing about where you leave a car. Portland Parks & Recreation publishes no parking information for this site: no lot, no capacity, no permit district, no warning. Columbia Park is a large park with other draws than pickleball, so a busy weekend is a reasonable thing to plan for, but that is our inference and not the department's statement.

Eight free courts, first-come and first-served, open dawn to dusk, and bring your own net — the city says so plainly, and with eight courts that is eight nets between everyone who turns up. The department asks players to limit a session to an hour when others are waiting, and its rules say a single player may not hold a court while a partner is on the way. Restrooms and drinking water are listed. Lighting is not mentioned, here or anywhere else on the city's pickleball page, so we do not know whether these courts can be played after dark and have not guessed.

Pier Park has four pickleball courts and one distinction no other outdoor site in Portland can claim: the city names what they are made of. Everywhere else the department writes "hard courts", which sorts a court into a category without naming a material — asphalt, concrete and acrylic are all hard — and this directory refuses that word as a surface for exactly that reason. Pier Park says "concrete", so concrete is what its record says. It is also one of the four parks Portland names as sanctioned pickleball sites, under its rule that striping goes only where courts stand roughly 300 to 600 feet from homes.

10325 N Lombard St, Portland, OR 97203 — the same street as Columbia Park and a shade under three miles further north-west along it, out towards St. Johns. Both are in the N sextant of Portland's grid and both were matched to Multnomah County by the Census geocoder. As at every other venue on this site, the parks department publishes nothing at all about parking here, so we have nothing verified to tell you about it.

Four free courts on concrete, with permanent lines, open dawn to dusk on a first-come basis, and bring your own net. Four courts is a small site by the standards of Columbia and Sellwood, so the department's one-hour courtesy limit is more likely to matter here on a busy afternoon. The amenities line lists restrooms — and, unlike the other outdoor parks in this set, does not mention drinking water. That is an absence in the city's list rather than a statement that there is none, so we record restrooms and leave water unclaimed. Lighting is not mentioned.

Sellwood Park has eight pickleball courts, tying it with Columbia Park as the largest year-round pickleball site in Portland, and it is the third of the four parks the city names as sanctioned pickleball locations. The courts are hard-surfaced with permanent lines and free to play. What makes Sellwood the useful one on the east side is simple arithmetic: it is the only eight-court site south of the river's east bank, and the next largest anywhere in the inner south-east is Laurelhurst's two.

7987 SE Grand Ave, Portland, OR 97202, in the south-east sextant, out at the southern end of the city's east side. The Census geocoder matched the address and placed it in Multnomah County. Portland Parks & Recreation publishes no parking guidance for the site — no lot, no street-parking note, no permit district — which is the case at all eleven venues in this city and is worth saying every time rather than once.

Eight free courts, dawn to dusk, first come first served, and bring your own net. The city's courtesy rules apply here as everywhere: an hour when others are waiting, no holding a court for an absent partner, and games to eleven, win by two. Restrooms and drinking water are listed among the amenities. Lighting is not stated anywhere on the department's pickleball page, so whether these eight courts can be used after dusk is unverified — and dusk is the operative limit, because the courts are open dawn to dusk rather than to a clock time.

Two courts, and both of them exist only for pickleball. Laurelhurst Park is one of three Portland sites the city describes as 'pickleball only' — the others are Gabriel Park and Hillside Park — and one of only two where nets are included. That combination is rarer than the court count suggests. Across all six free park sites in this city, twenty-one of the twenty-nine courts require you to bring your own net; Laurelhurst is part of the small remainder where a paddle and a ball are the whole kit list. The courts are hard-surfaced with permanent lines and free.

3789 SE Oak St, Portland, OR 97214, in the inner south-east, and matched by the Census geocoder to Multnomah County. Oak Street is a residential east-side street rather than an arterial, which is a fact about the address and not a claim about what you will find when you get there — Portland Parks & Recreation publishes no parking information for this venue, as it publishes none for any of the eleven.

Two courts, free, nets included, permanent lines, dawn to dusk, first come first served. Two courts is the second-smallest pickleball site in the city, so the department's request to limit play to an hour when others are waiting is likely to be the difference between playing and watching on a good evening. Restrooms and drinking water are listed. Lighting is not stated. Note that Laurelhurst is not one of the four parks Portland names as its sanctioned pickleball sites — those are Columbia, Pier, Sellwood and Gabriel — which does not make it less official, but is a reminder that the department distinguishes between where pickleball is provided and where it has been formally sited under its noise rule.

Gabriel Park is the best-equipped free pickleball site in Portland on the evidence the city publishes: six courts, described as 'pickleball only', with permanent lines and nets included, at no cost. It is the only venue in the city that is both a named sanctioned pickleball park and a dedicated, nets-included site — Columbia, Pier and Sellwood are sanctioned but shared-kit, Laurelhurst and Hillside are dedicated but smaller. If the question is where to send someone who owns a paddle and nothing else, this is the answer, and it is the largest such site in the city by a factor of three.

4508 SW Nevada St, Portland, OR 97219, in the south-west sextant — one of only three venues in this set on the west side of the river, along with Hillside Park and Southwest Community Center. The Census geocoder matched the address to Multnomah County. Southwest Community Center, the city's largest indoor site, is about 250 metres away — the closest pairing of an outdoor and an indoor pickleball venue anywhere in this directory. No parking information is published by the parks department for this or any other Portland venue, and Gabriel is a large multi-use park, so arriving with a plan B for the car is sensible rather than pessimistic.

Six free courts with nets already provided, dawn to dusk, first come first served. Six is enough that the one-hour courtesy limit is less likely to bite than at Laurelhurst or Hillside, and the dedicated striping means you are not negotiating with tennis players for the space. Restrooms and drinking water are listed among the amenities. Lighting is not stated — not here and not at any Portland venue — so evening play in the darker half of the year is an open question rather than a no.

One court. Hillside Park is the smallest pickleball venue in this directory anywhere, and it is here for the same reason the eight-court sites are: the city states it. The single court is described as 'pickleball only' with the courts at Laurelhurst and Gabriel, and it is free. It is also the only outdoor entry on Portland's pickleball page with no amenities line at all — where the other five parks list restrooms, and four of them water, Hillside's entry simply ends after "bring your own net". That silence is recorded as unverified rather than as an absence.

653 NW Culpepper Terrace, Portland, OR 97210, in the north-west sextant, up in the west hills — the Census geocoder matched the address to Multnomah County. Culpepper Terrace is a hillside residential street, which the address itself tells you, and the parks department publishes no parking guidance here any more than it does elsewhere. A single-court site on a hill street is not somewhere to arrive with a group and no fallback.

One free court, dedicated to pickleball, with your own net required, dawn to dusk, first come first served. With one court, Portland's rule about limiting play to an hour when others are waiting is the whole etiquette of the place, along with its companion rule that a single player may not hold a court while a partner is on the way. No restrooms are listed. No water is listed. No lighting is stated. This is the venue in Portland where what the city does not publish matters most, because there is the least here to absorb a surprise.

Four indoor courts, and one of the four Portland community centres that take drop-in pickleball players at $6 for adults and $5 for seniors. It is the second-largest indoor site in the city after Southwest Community Center's five. In a city whose outdoor courts run dawn to dusk on surfaces the parks department warns are slippery when wet, the fourteen indoor courts spread across these four centres are what makes the sport a year-round proposition, and this is nearly a third of them.

740 SE 106th Ave, Portland, OR 97216, in the south-east sextant well out towards the city's eastern edge — matched by the Census geocoder to Multnomah County. It is the easternmost venue in this set. As at all eleven Portland venues, the parks department publishes nothing about parking.

Four courts indoors and a published price — $6 for adults, $5 for seniors, per drop-in session — which is the first cost figure any operator in this directory has stated in five cities of trying. What the city does not publish on its pickleball page is the schedule: it lists the count and the price and then directs drop-in players to the community centre's own page for times. So treat four courts as what exists rather than as what is free on a given afternoon, and check the centre before travelling. The surface is not stated here, unlike the wood floors at Southwest and St. Johns. Neither is whether nets are provided, and we have not assumed it.

Five indoor courts on a wood floor — the largest indoor pickleball site in Portland and one of only three venues in this city with a surface we can publish. It appears twice on the city's pickleball page: once under indoor courts with a count and a drop-in price, and again under registered activities as "Indoor wood courts, permanent lines, nets provided". From that second listing we take the wood and the restrooms, which are facts about the building and true whichever door you came through, and not the nets, which describe what a particular registered programme puts out.

6820 SW 45th Ave, Portland, OR 97219, in the south-west sextant, and matched by the Census geocoder to Multnomah County. It is about 250 metres from Gabriel Park's six dedicated courts — near enough to walk between them — which makes this corner of south-west Portland the only part of the city where a large free outdoor site and the largest indoor site sit within easy reach of each other — useful in a city where the weather decides which one you want. No parking information is published.

Five courts indoors, wood floor, permanent lines, $6 for adults and $5 for seniors as a drop-in. There is also a registered pickleball programme here, booked through an ActiveNet account, which the city says takes no court reservations. The schedule for either is on the centre's own page rather than the city's pickleball page, so check before you travel. Restrooms and drinking water are listed. Whether nets are out for drop-in play is not something the city states, and we have declined to infer it from the registered programme's description.

Two indoor courts on a wood floor, the smallest of Portland's four drop-in community centres, at the same $6 adult and $5 senior rate as the others. Like Southwest Community Center it is listed twice on the city's pickleball page — once with its court count and price, once under registered activities as "Indoor wood courts, permanent lines, nets provided" — and the same narrow reading applies here: the wood floor and the restrooms are properties of the building and are recorded, the nets describe a programme and are not.

8427 N Central St, Portland, OR 97203, in the north sextant, matched by the Census geocoder to Multnomah County. It shares its postcode with Columbia Park and Pier Park, and sits between the two of them — which makes this stretch of North Portland the one part of the city where twelve free outdoor courts and an indoor room are all within a short distance of each other. Nothing about parking is published.

Two courts, wood floor, permanent lines, drop-in at $6 for adults and $5 for seniors, plus a registered programme booked through ActiveNet that takes no court reservations. Two courts is small enough that the schedule matters more than the count, and the schedule is on the centre's own page rather than the city's pickleball page. Restrooms and drinking water are listed. Nets for drop-in play are unverified.

Three indoor courts at the standard Portland drop-in rate of $6 for adults and $5 for seniors. Montavilla is the plainest entry of the four community centres on the city's pickleball page: a name, an address, a court count and a price, with no second listing under registered activities and so no statement about the floor, the nets or the amenities. That makes it the indoor venue about which we know the least, and the record reflects that rather than borrowing detail from the centres that say more.

8219 NE Glisan St, Portland, OR 97220, in the north-east sextant on an east-west arterial, matched by the Census geocoder to Multnomah County. It is the only venue in this set in the NE quadrant. The parks department publishes no parking information here, as at every other Portland venue.

Three courts indoors at $6 adult and $5 senior per drop-in session, with the schedule on the community centre's own page rather than the city's pickleball page. Beyond that, the honest answer is that the city has not said: no surface, no note on nets, no amenities line. Unlike Southwest and St. Johns, Montavilla has no registered-programme entry that might have told us about the floor. Three courts is the middle of Portland's indoor range — more than St. Johns, fewer than East Portland and Southwest.

Sixteen outdoor courts — the largest single venue in this directory, in any city — and the one where the number needs its sentence read to the end. Portland Parks & Recreation states "16 outdoor hard courts, permanent lines, nets provided", and then: "Available from mid June until early September." Pickleball here is a registered summer programme, booked through an ActiveNet account, with no court reservations taken. The courts and their permanent lines are not seasonal; the access to them for pickleball is. We publish the sixteen rather than hiding them, and we publish the season alongside, because a court count without its availability is the kind of true number that misleads.

324 NE 12th Ave, Portland, OR 97232, in the north-east sextant just across the river from the city centre — the most central venue in this set, and matched by the Census geocoder to Multnomah County. It is about a mile and a half from Laurelhurst Park's two dedicated courts, which is the nearest year-round alternative on this side of the river. No parking information is published for it.

In season, sixteen outdoor hard courts with permanent lines and nets provided, run as mixer activities requiring an ActiveNet account and pre-registration, with no court reservations. Out of season, this is not a pickleball venue. What the city does not state is the price: registration goes through ActiveNet, which prices per activity, and no figure appears on the pickleball page — so the cost here reads "not verified yet" rather than free. Restrooms and drinking water are listed. Lighting, as everywhere in Portland, is not mentioned. We have also left the venue type blank: this is a municipal tennis centre, and the nearest options available to us are park, club and community centre, none of which is true.

Baileywick Park is the only place in this directory's Raleigh set where you can play pickleball under a roof, and the only one where the city's two inventories disagree about how much pickleball there is. The park's own page lists three hard courts — Court A covered, Court B covered centre, Court C uncovered — and the weekly schedule puts pickleball on Courts A and B. Raleigh Parks' pickleball page says the park has six pickleball courts; the GIS Athletic Courts layer, which holds polygons for A and B and none for C, adds up to four. We publish six, because the pickleball page is the department speaking directly to players and its figure reconciles with the citywide total of 44 that the same page states, and we have flagged the venue for a re-check rather than pretending the question is settled. The courts are lit. They are also genuinely shared: basketball open play, a youth basketball league and futsal all appear on the same three courts across the week, which is why pickleball here runs to published windows rather than whenever you turn up.

Baileywick is in the far north of the city at 9501 Baileywick Road, and it is one of very few Raleigh park pages that tells you where to park: the page names a lot at that same address. A paved walking trail runs from the Baileywick Road entrance, loops behind the playground and comes out at the parking lot. There is a restroom facility on site. The park also carries the .6-mile Baileywick Greenway Trail, which connects Strickland Road to Baileywick Road through the park.

Check the clock and the closure notice before you go. Pickleball has Courts A and B on Monday to Friday from noon to 4 p.m., Saturday from 3 to 9 p.m. and Sunday from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m.; outside those windows the courts belong to basketball or futsal. Walk-up play is first-come, first-served, but Raleigh Parks is explicit that walk-up use is not allowed on courts scheduled for a league or programmed activity and that the scheduled activity has priority. The closure matters more here than it usually would: the department posted on 24 August 2026 that Baileywick Park Pavilion-Court A is closed for repairs, with no reopening date given, and Court A is one of the two courts pickleball uses. Nothing published says whether nets are provided, so take one if you have one, and nothing published gives a surface.

Carolina Pines is a full neighbourhood park in south Raleigh with a community centre attached, and its pickleball is painted onto its tennis courts rather than built for the purpose. Raleigh Parks lists four pickleball courts here and marks them lit; the department's note for this location is unusually direct about what that means in practice — "Tennis courts with pickleball lines - need to bring of borrow a net". The park's own page records three tennis courts with push-button lighting from dusk to 10 p.m. and no backboards, which is the surface the pickleball lines sit on. This is the second location in Raleigh where the city's two inventories differ: the GIS Athletic Courts layer records three pickleball courts against the pickleball page's four. We publish four, for the same reason as at Baileywick — the pickleball page reconciles with the citywide total of 44 — and the venue is flagged for a re-check. Around the courts the park also holds two unlit volleyball courts, three lit ball fields, and a new accessible playground.

The park is at 2305 Lake Wheeler Road, postcode 27603, south-west of downtown. Raleigh Parks publishes no parking guidance for these courts, so we cannot tell you where the lot is, how big it is, or whether it fills — only that the park page does not say. There is a restroom on site, recorded in the city's park amenities inventory. The community centre keeps its own hours, Monday to Friday 10 a.m. to 9 p.m., Saturday 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. and Sunday 1 to 6 p.m., which are not the same thing as the court hours.

Bring a net, because the city tells you to. Beyond that, expect a shared surface: pickleball lines over tennis courts means the lines you are playing to are not the only lines on the ground, and it means the courts can be in use for tennis when you arrive. The lighting is push-button rather than on a timer, according to the park page's court entry, so you switch it on rather than waiting for it — and it runs to 10 p.m. like the rest of the city's lit courts. Raleigh Parks' guidelines apply here as everywhere: sign in or place a paddle, games to 11 and win by 2, and all four players come off at the end of each game so the next four can go on. No source states a surface material for these courts, and none states a fee either way.

Fred Fletcher Park sits just north-west of downtown Raleigh on ground with a history the city publishes: it is the former campus of the Methodist Home for Children, bought by the City in 1982. For pickleball it is one of the smaller and plainer entries in the Raleigh set — two courts, lines painted on the park's tennis courts, and no lights. The absence of lights is stated rather than merely missing: Raleigh Parks marks this location No in the Lights column of its pickleball table, and the park's own page independently records its tennis courts as having no lights and no backboard. That makes it one of only two daylight-only pickleball locations in the city, alongside Southgate Park. The rest of the park is a well-equipped neighbourhood green: an outdoor basketball court, a picnic shelter with capacity for 36 to 60, a softball field, a multipurpose field of 300 by 195 feet, a playground for ages 2 to 12 on a sand surface, a water garden and wetland, and walking paths.

The park has two frontages and the city uses both. Its own page gives the address as 820 Clay Street and 805 Washington Street, postcode 27605, and notes entrances off St. Mary's Street and Glenwood Avenue; the city's park amenities inventory records 805 Washington Street. We publish 820 Clay Street and list the other as an alternative rather than treating either as wrong. Be careful with a third address: Raleigh Parks' pickleball table lists this park at "514 Method Road", which is the address of Method Community Park in the row below it — a duplicated cell, not a second location. No parking guidance is published, and no restroom is recorded here.

Daylight play only, on tennis courts. There are two pickleball courts' worth of lines here and no floodlights, so in winter the usable window is short. Nothing published says whether nets are provided, so assume you are bringing one. Nothing published gives a surface material or its condition. The park is central enough that the courts share the site with a good deal else — basketball, a softball field, a large multipurpose field and a playground — so the hard courts are one small part of a busy neighbourhood park rather than a destination for pickleball in the way Sanderford Road is. Raleigh Parks' sign-up guidelines apply: place a paddle or sign in, games to 11 and win by 2, and the whole four come off at the end of each game.

Jaycee Park is a community park on Wade Avenue, west of downtown, and its pickleball is two courts of lines on the park's tennis courts. Raleigh Parks marks the location as lit, so unlike Fred Fletcher it is usable in the evening — the city's lit courts run on a timer to 10 p.m. The park is best known locally for other things: its dog run is described at length on the city's page, with an accessible sidewalk connecting it to the parking lot on Wade Avenue and benches, trash cans and a dog waste station inside. A community centre shares the site and keeps its own hours. For a player, the honest summary is that this is a neighbourhood park where pickleball is one of several things happening rather than the main event, and where the two courts are shared with tennis. It is one of nine lit Raleigh locations, and one of six where the pickleball is painted onto tennis courts.

2405 Wade Avenue, postcode 27607. This is one of the few Raleigh park pages that mentions parking at all, though it does so while describing the route to the dog run rather than to the courts: it notes a parking lot on Wade Avenue and says ample parking is provided on both sides of the dog run. No capacity, time limit or permit information is published. A restroom is recorded on site in the city's park amenities inventory.

Two courts, lit, shared with tennis. Nothing published states whether nets are provided at this location, so bring one rather than assume — the city says so explicitly at only two of its eleven locations and this is not one of them. Nothing published gives the surface material or when it was last done. Raleigh Parks' rotation guidelines apply here as at every city facility: there is a sign-up procedure, each player signs in or places a paddle, games are singles or doubles to 11 and win by 2, and at the end of each game all four players leave the court so the next four on the list can play. If you are coming as a group and want to stay together, the guidelines ask you to skip to the next fully open quadrant on the sign-up rather than break into an existing one.

Method Community Park holds six permanent pickleball courts, which puts it joint second in Raleigh behind Sanderford Road, and it is one of only three locations in the city where the courts are built for pickleball rather than painted onto something else. Both of the city's inventories agree on the number, which is not true everywhere in this set. The park's own page states it plainly — "6 courts", "Lighting on timer from dusk to 10 p.m.", "Has backboards" — and adds that players are asked to follow all posted rules regarding rotating courts. Raleigh Parks marks the location "Drop in only, no reservations", which is worth more than it sounds: at locations that do take bookings you can arrive to find the courts already claimed, and here you cannot. The park shares its address with the Method Road Community Centre, one of the thirteen sites running the city's indoor pickleball programme, and the centre's gym can be rented for what the city's page describes as three pickle courts and one volleyball court at $85 an hour.

514 Method Road, postcode 27607, west of downtown near the NC State campus. Raleigh Parks publishes no parking guidance for the courts, and no restroom is recorded for the park in the city's amenities inventory — though the community centre on the same site keeps public hours of its own. If you are navigating, note that the city's pickleball table also lists Fred Fletcher Park at this address by mistake; Fred Fletcher is a different park about two miles away.

Six permanent courts with backboards, lit on a timer from dusk to 10 p.m., and no way for anyone to book them out from under you. Raleigh Parks' sign-up system is the thing to understand before arriving alone: there is a game sign-up procedure at each facility, players sign in or place a paddle, games are singles or doubles to 11 points and win by 2, and at the conclusion of every game all four players leave the court and the next four on the sign-up go on. That is what makes a permanent-court site like this one workable for a single player in a way a shared tennis court usually is not. What the city does not publish here is a surface material, whether nets are provided on the outdoor courts, or any fee — the $3 session and $15 four-month pass it advertises are for the indoor programme in the gym, not for these courts.

North Hills Park has six permanent pickleball courts in north Raleigh, and along with Method Community Park it is one of the two locations the city marks "Drop in only, no reservations" — the courts cannot be booked out ahead of you. The city's pickleball page and its GIS court inventory agree on the count, and so does the commercial dataset this directory started from, which is a rarer alignment than it ought to be. The park page carries a pickleball section of its own and gives an email address, pickleball@raleighnc.gov, for questions; it also states that court reservations are not offered during open play. The courts are lit, though that is the one thing about this venue that may not be true on the day you read it. Raleigh Parks began a lighting upgrade here on 24 August 2026 and closed the courts; daytime play reopened on Wednesday 2 September and the department targeted 8 September for completion, with night play unavailable until the work finishes.

100 Chowan Circle, postcode 27609, in the North Hills area north of the Beltline. No parking guidance is published for the courts. A restroom is recorded at this park in the city's amenities inventory, which is not the case at most of the Raleigh locations in this set. Do not confuse this park with the private North Hills Club nearby, which is a different venue and is not verified here.

Six permanent courts, drop-in only, and — assuming the upgrade has finished — lights on a timer to 10 p.m. The department's sign-up rules apply: sign in or place a paddle, games to 11 and win by 2, and all four players come off at the end of each game so the next four can go on. The park page's own note that reservations are not offered during open play is worth reading alongside that: the rotation is the queueing system, so a group of four cannot hold a court indefinitely. What is not published is the surface material, whether nets are provided outdoors, or any fee. Before an evening trip, check the park's status page — the lighting work was still listed as incomplete when we last read it on 3 September 2026.

Powell Drive Park is a neighbourhood park in south-west Raleigh with two pickleball courts, lines painted on its tennis courts, and lights. It is one of the six Raleigh locations where pickleball shares a tennis surface, and one of nine that are lit, so it works in the evening in a way Fred Fletcher and Southgate do not. Both the department's pickleball page and its GIS court inventory record two courts here, so there is no dispute about the number. The park page describes an outdoor basketball court with a concrete surface among its facilities, but publishes no surface for the tennis courts the pickleball lines sit on, so we do not state one. This is a small, ordinary, useful piece of municipal pickleball provision: two courts, lit, free of any published booking requirement, in a residential part of the city — and the city publishes very little else about it, which we would rather say than pad out.

740 Powell Drive, postcode 27606. Raleigh Parks publishes no parking guidance for this park, and no restroom is recorded here in the city's park amenities inventory. If facilities matter to you, the nearest verified restrooms in this set are at Carolina Pines Park and Jaycee Park.

Two courts of pickleball lines over tennis, lit to 10 p.m. on the city's timer. Expect to share: a tennis player has as much claim on the surface as you do, and with only two courts a queue builds quickly. Raleigh Parks' guidelines are the arbiter — a sign-up procedure at each facility, sign in or place your paddle, games singles or doubles to 11 and win by 2, and all four players off at the end of each game. Groups who want to stay together are asked to skip to the next fully open quadrant on the sign-up rather than split an existing one. Nothing published says whether nets are provided at this location, and unlike Carolina Pines and Southgate the department does not tell you to bring your own either, so this is genuinely unknown rather than a hint — take a net if you can. No fee is published for the outdoor courts.

Roberts Park is in south-east Raleigh, close to the centre on East Martin Street, and it offers two lit pickleball courts painted onto its tennis courts. The department's pickleball page and its GIS court inventory agree on the count. What makes Roberts more useful than its two courts suggest is that it is one of only five locations in the Raleigh set where the city's park amenities inventory records a restroom, and it is close in — a genuinely central option in a city whose largest pickleball sites are all some way out. The park also has an outdoor basketball court. As at the other tennis-striped locations, the pickleball lines share a surface with tennis, so the courts are not reserved for one sport and the lines under your feet are not all yours. Nothing published tells us the surface material or its condition, and nothing published states a fee for the outdoor courts.

1300 E. Martin Street, postcode 27610. No parking guidance is published for this park. A restroom is recorded on site in the city's park amenities inventory. A community centre shares the site and keeps its own published hours, which are not the same as court hours.

Two lit courts, shared with tennis, on the city's standard terms. The lights run on a timer to 10 p.m. Raleigh Parks' rotation guidelines apply: a sign-up procedure at each facility, sign in or place your paddle, games to 11 and win by 2, and the full four come off at the end of each game so the next four can go on. With two courts and a central location, expect that queue to matter more here than at a ten-court site. The city does not publish whether nets are provided, so bring one. It does not publish a surface. And it does not publish a fee for outdoor play — the $3 and $15 prices Raleigh advertises are for the indoor community-centre programme, which is a different thing at different sites and does not apply to walking up to these courts.

Sanderford Road Park is the largest pickleball site in Raleigh and the largest in this directory's Wake County coverage: ten permanent courts, lit, on a single site in the south-east of the city. That is nearly a quarter of the city's 44 outdoor courts in one park. Everything we can check agrees on the number — Raleigh Parks' pickleball page, the department's GIS court inventory, and independent pickleball listings all give ten — which is worth saying because two other Raleigh venues in this set do not have that agreement. The department marks the location as permanent courts rather than lines on a tennis surface, and unlike Method and North Hills it does not mark it drop-in only; the park's own page states that court reservations are available here, so some of the ten may be booked when you arrive. The park also holds an outdoor basketball court with four hoops on a concrete surface. If you are new to the city and want the best odds of getting a game, this is the site to try first.

2623 Sanderford Road, postcode 27610, in south-east Raleigh. Both of the city's records give that address; note that some third-party listings show 2823, which does not match either city source. Raleigh Parks publishes no parking guidance for the courts, and no restroom is recorded for this park in the city's amenities inventory — worth planning around at a site where you may be staying for several games.

Ten permanent courts is enough that the sign-up system does real work. Raleigh Parks' guidelines describe a game sign-up procedure at each facility: players sign in or place a paddle in a quadrant of four, games are singles or doubles to 11 points and win by 2, and at the conclusion of each game all four players leave the court and the next four go on. Groups wanting to stay together are asked to skip to the next fully open quadrant rather than break one up. Because reservations are available at this location, check the department's monthly pickleball calendar before travelling — a booked court is a court you cannot rotate onto. The lights run on the city's timer to 10 p.m. No surface material is published for these courts, no fee is published, and the city does not state whether nets are provided, so take one.

Southgate Park is the outlier in Raleigh's set, and the one place where the city publishes a surface. Its two pickleball courts are lines painted on basketball courts rather than on tennis courts — the only location in the city where that is true — and the GIS court inventory records the surface as asphalt, the single populated surface value across every pickleball court polygon in all eleven Raleigh parks. It is also one of only two unlit locations, along with Fred Fletcher Park, so play here is a daylight proposition. Raleigh Parks is direct about the practical consequence of painting pickleball onto a basketball court: its note for this location says you need to bring your own net. Between the shared basketball surface, the absence of lights and the missing net, this is the most improvised pickleball in the Raleigh set, and it is listed here because the city lists it rather than because it is anyone's first choice.

1801 Proctor Street, postcode 27610, in south-east Raleigh. Two city sources — the department's pickleball page and the park's own page — give the street as Proctor Street, while the city's GIS park amenities inventory records it as Proctor Rd; we publish what the two park-facing pages say. No parking guidance is published, and no restroom is recorded for this park in the city's amenities inventory.

Bring a net, and come in daylight. Those are the two things the city tells you outright about this location, and both are unusual enough to be worth repeating: Raleigh Parks says to bring your own net here, and marks the location unlit. The surface is asphalt, which the GIS inventory states and which is a harder, rougher surface than the acrylic most dedicated courts use. The lines sit on basketball courts, so expect to share with basketball rather than tennis. Raleigh Parks' sign-up guidelines apply here as everywhere — sign in or place a paddle, games to 11 and win by 2, all four players off at the end of each game — though with two courts and no lights the practical constraint is more likely to be the daylight than the queue. No fee is published for these courts.

Tarboro Road Park sits close to downtown Raleigh on North Tarboro Street and offers two lit pickleball courts, painted onto the park's tennis courts. The department's pickleball page, its GIS court inventory and the commercial dataset this directory started from all give the same count of two, so there is nothing in dispute here. The site is busier than its two courts suggest: a community centre shares the park, and so does the Saint Monica Teen Center, each keeping its own published hours. That makes Tarboro Road one of the more central places to play in a city whose biggest pickleball sites are all further out, and one of nine lit Raleigh locations, so it is usable after work. The trade-off is the one common to six of the eleven Raleigh locations — the courts belong to tennis as much as to pickleball, and with only two of them a queue forms quickly.

121 N. Tarboro Street, postcode 27610, just east of downtown. Raleigh Parks publishes no parking guidance for the courts. No restroom is recorded for the park itself in the city's amenities inventory, though the community centre and teen centre on the same site keep public hours of their own. Note that the park's page carries several separate sets of opening hours — for the park, the community centre and the teen centre — and none of them is a statement of when the outdoor courts are available, so we do not publish court hours here.

Two lit courts over tennis lines, on the city's usual terms. The lights run on a timer until 10 p.m. Raleigh Parks' rotation guidelines govern play: a sign-up procedure at each facility, sign in or place your paddle, games singles or doubles to 11 points and win by 2, and all four players leave the court at the end of each game so the next four can go on. Groups are asked to skip to the next fully open quadrant on the sign-up rather than break one up. The city does not state whether nets are provided at this location, so bring one. It does not publish a surface material for these courts, or a fee — the $3 session and $15 four-month pass it advertises are for indoor open play at its community centres, and the centre on this site is one of the thirteen that runs it.

Green Lake Park East is the largest pickleball site Seattle Parks records, with eight courts striped for tennis and pickleball on the east side of the lake, and it is the only one in the city running an organised open-play programme. That programme is what makes it different from every other entry in this directory. Since 1 October 2025 the city has staffed scheduled sessions here with ambassadors who arrange games and run a paddle stacking system, which is a rotation queue: you put your paddle in the stack and get called into the next game rather than needing to arrive as a group of four. It was set up as a one-year pilot, so its future beyond autumn 2026 is not something we can tell you. The courts sit inside Green Lake Park, which is one of the busiest parks in Seattle, and the parking that serves them serves the whole lake path rather than the courts specifically. It is also the venue where our imported record was most wrong, which is worth stating on the page rather than quietly fixing. The commercial dataset we started from listed Green Lake as four courts, two of them indoor. Seattle Parks records eight courts, all outdoor, and there is no indoor pickleball at Green Lake at all. That is a doubling of the court count and the invention of two indoor courts in a city that has none verified, and it is the clearest single illustration of why nothing here publishes until a named source has confirmed it.

Seattle Parks records dedicated parking at this site and gives the address as 7201 E Green Lake Dr N. Be careful with that: the lot belongs to Green Lake Park as a whole, and the park draws walkers, runners and rowers all day, so a dedicated lot existing is not the same as a space being free when you arrive. The city publishes no capacity or time-limit information for it and we have not checked restrictions on the ground, so read the posted signs. An all-year restroom is recorded on site.

Eight courts with nets provided, no lights, and tennis lines under your feet. If you are coming alone or as a pair, come inside one of the open-play windows — Monday 8 to 10 a.m., Wednesday 1 to 3 p.m., Saturday 9 to 11 a.m., or Sunday 4 to 6 p.m. — because that is when the rotation runs and when getting into a game does not depend on who you brought. Outside those hours it is first come, first served like everywhere else. With no lighting recorded here, play ends when the light does, which in a Seattle December is early.

Gilman Playground in Ballard carries four courts striped for tennis and pickleball, and it is one of three Seattle sites where the city has formally restricted when you may play. In September 2025 Seattle Parks, working with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections, ran noise studies at this location and found play producing sound levels above the limits set in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08. The result was a posted schedule with real enforcement behind it rather than a request for consideration. That history is worth knowing before you turn up, because it shapes both when the courts are open and how the neighbours are likely to feel about a loud evening game.

The address Seattle Parks records is 923 NW 54th St, and the city records street parking rather than a dedicated lot — this is a residential Ballard block, and no capacity, permit or time-limit information is published for it. A seasonal restroom is recorded, which means do not count on it out of season. We have not verified parking restrictions on the ground; read the signs.

Four courts, nets provided, and no lights recorded, which matters more here than elsewhere because the posted hours run to 10 p.m. and nothing illuminates the court after dusk. Play is permitted 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays. Those hours are enforced: a violation captured on timestamped photo or video results in a lock fitted to the courts for at least thirty days, and repeat violations make the lock permanent, after which the courts open only when staff are on site to unlock them. For context on how unusual that is: of the twenty-four verified Seattle venues, only three carry a city-imposed curfew, and Gilman is the smallest of them by court count. Nineteen of the twenty-four have no lighting recorded at all, so for most of the city the limit on evening play is the sunset rather than the council.

Laurelhurst Playfield holds a single dedicated pickleball court — one of only three dedicated courts among the twenty-four Seattle venues we have verified, with every other site striped over tennis or shared with basketball or badminton. Being dedicated is the good news and being one court is the bad news, and the second is the more useful fact when you are deciding whether to drive here. It is also one of three Seattle locations where the city imposed restricted hours in September 2025 after noise studies with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections found play exceeding the limits in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08. There is one more thing worth knowing, and it is a correction rather than a feature. Our imported record placed this venue at 4339 NE 43rd St. The city's own parcel record puts it at 4544 NE 41st St, two blocks away, and the city is describing land it owns. We have taken the municipal address and left the imported one visible in our change log rather than overwriting history, because a directory that silently corrects itself is asking to be trusted on exactly the thing it just got wrong.

Seattle Parks records the address as 4544 NE 41st St, which corrects the address our imported record carried — it had this venue two blocks away on NE 43rd St. Dedicated parking is recorded on site, along with an all-year restroom. The city publishes no capacity or restriction detail, and we have not checked it in person.

One court, nets provided, no lights. A single court means one game at a time, so on a good weekend afternoon expect either a wait or a rotation negotiated between whoever is there. Play is permitted 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays, and those hours carry the same enforcement as the other two restricted sites: timestamped evidence of play outside them leads to a lock for a minimum of thirty days, permanent on repeat.

Mt. Baker Park carries four courts striped for tennis and pickleball, and it is the only one of the three restricted-hours sites that also has lights — which is an odd combination worth understanding before you plan an evening around it. The city recorded lighting here, and then in September 2025 capped play at 10 p.m. after noise studies with the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections found sound levels above the limits in Seattle Municipal Code chapter 25.08. So the lights exist and the clock still stops. Of the five lit venues among our twenty-four verified Seattle sites, this is the one where the lights are least useful late. Our imported record also had this venue's address as a street with no number — just Lake Park Dr S — which is the kind of gap that looks harmless until someone tries to drive to it. The city's parcel record supplied 2521, and that is the number shown above.

The address Seattle Parks records is 2521 Lake Park Dr S; our imported record had the street with no number, and the city's own parcel record supplied it. Street parking rather than a dedicated lot, on a residential block above Lake Washington, with an all-year restroom recorded on site. No permit or time-limit information is published and we have not verified restrictions in person.

Four courts with nets provided and lights, open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. at weekends and city-observed holidays. The enforcement here is the same as at Gilman and Laurelhurst: play documented outside posted hours with timestamped visual evidence results in a lock for at least thirty days, and further violations make it permanent. If you want lit courts without a curfew, Bitter Lake Playfield and Rainier Beach Playfield are the two larger lit sites with no restricted-hours order recorded against them. One practical note on the curfew that applies to all three restricted sites: the enforcement trigger is documented evidence rather than a complaint, so it is timestamped photos and video that lead to a lock, not annoyance on its own. That distinction is in the city's own announcement and it is the reason the posted hours are worth taking literally here in a way they are not at an unlit park that empties at dusk anyway.

Bitter Lake Playfield holds eight courts striped for tennis and pickleball under lights, which makes it one of exactly two sites in Seattle offering both the largest court count and evening play. Between it and Rainier Beach Playfield sit sixteen of the ninety-two verified courts in the city, and they carry most of the practical capacity for playing here once the light goes. It is also the venue our imported data handled worst. The commercial dataset we started from held two separate Bitter Lake entries: a community centre with three indoor courts, and a second row claiming eleven courts of which three were indoor. Seattle Parks records one pickleball site at this address, with eight courts, all outdoor. We matched the outdoor row and left the community centre alone, because the centre is a building with its own indoor courts and merging the two would have invented a fifteen-court complex that does not exist anywhere except in a spreadsheet.

Seattle Parks records the address as 13035 Linden Ave N and gives this site dedicated parking rather than street parking, which among the twenty-four verified venues puts it in the better-served half. The restroom is recorded as seasonal, so it is not something to count on outside the warm months. No capacity, permit or time-limit information is published for the parking, and none of it has been checked on the ground.

Eight courts, nets provided, and lights: the fullest combination available in Seattle on the city's own record. The courts are shared with tennis, so expect tennis lines underfoot and the possibility of a booked court, which is true of eighteen of the twenty-five sites Seattle Parks lists.
